Recall of Day 2 — laws and regulations (15 minutes)

  • Hierarchy of obligations: laws and regulations (mandatory) → contractual standards (PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard), binding through the merchant agreement) → voluntary frameworks (NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) CSF (Cybersecurity Framework), ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission) 27001, CIS (Center for Internet Security) Controls) → internal policies.
  • The five texts that apply to Érable Cycles: PIPEDA (federal private-sector privacy law), Québec Law 25 (modernized Private Sector Act), GDPR (partly — only the data of customers located in the EU (European Union), Article 3(2)(a)), PCI DSS v4.0.1 (by contract; hosted payment page and P2PE (point-to-point encryption) terminals keep most systems out of the CDE (cardholder data environment)) and CASL (the newsletter is a CEM (commercial electronic message)).
  • Breach duties: PIPEDA — report to the OPC (Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada) and notify individuals when there is a real risk of significant harm, keep every breach record 24 months; Law 25 — notify the CAI (Commission d’accès à l’information du Québec) and the persons when there is a risk of serious injury, keep the incident register at least 5 years; GDPR — notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours.
  • CASL: consent (express or implied), sender identification and a working unsubscribe honoured within 10 business days; the sender must be able to prove consent.
  • Retention — the bridge to tonight: the CRA (Canada Revenue Agency) sets a minimum (6 years for tax records); the privacy laws set a maximum (personal information only as long as necessary). Tonight’s retention schedule respects both.
  • Bill C-36 (Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act) — checked today, November 3, 2026: still at second reading in the House of Commons, no activity since first reading on June 15, 2026. It is proposed only; PIPEDA remains the law in force.
1

NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 — Functions, Tiers and Profiles

≈ 10 min · Lesson 1 of 6
Learning objectives — after this lesson you can:
  • Name the six Functions of the CSF 2.0 and say what each one covers.
  • Explain the difference between a Function, a Category and a Subcategory.
  • Explain what Tiers measure and what a Current Profile and a Target Profile are.
  • Decide whether the CSF alone is enough for Érable Cycles (it is not: it is a framework of outcomes, not a checklist of settings).

1.1 What the CSF is and where it comes from

The NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) is a voluntary, free framework published by the NIST, an agency of the United States Department of Commerce. Version 2.0 was published on February 26, 2024 as NIST CSWP 29. Version 1.0 (2014) was written for operators of critical infrastructure; version 2.0 dropped that restriction from its title and is written for any organization of any size, which is why a 45-employee bicycle retailer can use it.

The CSF describes cybersecurity outcomes — results an organization wants to reach — not products to buy and not configuration settings to apply. It therefore answers the question “what should our security program achieve?”. The question “how exactly is a Windows laptop configured?” is answered by other documents (CIS (Center for Internet Security) Benchmarks, Microsoft baselines), which we meet in Lesson 3 and in Lab 3.

The framework has three components: the Core (the list of outcomes), the Tiers (how an organization governs and manages its cybersecurity risk) and the Organizational Profiles (the Core applied to one organization: where it is now and where it wants to be).

1.2 The Core: six Functions, 22 Categories, 106 Subcategories

The Core is organized in three levels. A Function is the highest level and names a broad outcome. A Category is a group of related outcomes inside a Function. A Subcategory is one specific, testable outcome. CSF 2.0 has 6 Functions, 22 Categories and 106 Subcategories. Each identifier is built from the Function code, the Category code and a number: GV.PO-01 means Function Govern, Category Policy, Subcategory 01.

Function (code)What it covers — in one sentenceExample CategoryWhere it appears in this course
Govern (GV) — new in 2.0The organization’s cybersecurity risk-management strategy, expectations and policy are established, communicated and monitored.GV.PO Policy · GV.RM Risk Management Strategy · GV.SC Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk ManagementLab 1 (requirements, policies), Lab 3 (administrative controls)
Identify (ID (identifier))The organization’s current cybersecurity risks are understood: assets, suppliers, vulnerabilities, improvements.ID.AM Asset Management · ID.RA Risk Assessment · ID.IM ImprovementLab 2 (asset inventory, assessment plan)
Protect (PR)Safeguards to manage the risks are used: access control, awareness, data security, platform security, infrastructure resilience.PR.AA Identity Management, Authentication and Access Control · PR.PS Platform Security · PR.DS Data SecurityLab 3 (configuration audit, controls verification)
Detect (DE)Possible attacks and compromises are found and analyzed.DE.CM Continuous Monitoring · DE.AE Adverse Event AnalysisLab 3 (logging, monitoring checks)
Respond (RS)Actions regarding a detected incident are taken: management, analysis, mitigation, reporting and communication.RS.MA Incident Management · RS.CO Incident Response Reporting and CommunicationProject (corrective-action plan; links to the breach duties of Day 2)
Recover (RC)Assets and operations affected by an incident are restored.RC.RP Incident Recovery Plan Execution · RC.CO Incident Recovery CommunicationLab 3 (backup exists and restore tested)

The Functions are not sequential steps. Govern informs the other five, and Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover run at the same time in a working program. The official figure draws Govern in the centre of a wheel for that reason.

1.3 Tiers: how risk is governed and managed

Tiers describe the rigor of an organization’s cybersecurity risk governance and management. There are four: Tier 1 — Partial (ad hoc, reactive), Tier 2 — Risk Informed (management approves practices, but they are not organization-wide policy), Tier 3 — Repeatable (formal policy, regularly updated practices) and Tier 4 — Adaptive (continuous improvement, lessons learned, predictive indicators). NIST states that Tiers are not maturity levels to climb for their own sake: an organization selects the Tier that matches its risk appetite, its legal obligations and its resources. For an SME (small or medium-sized enterprise) such as Érable Cycles, Tier 2 moving towards Tier 3 is a realistic target.

1.4 Organizational Profiles: a Profile is a small conformity assessment

An Organizational Profile is the Core applied to one organization. The Current Profile records which outcomes are achieved today and to what degree; the Target Profile records the outcomes the organization wants to achieve, chosen from its legal obligations (Lab 1), its risks and its business goals. The difference between the two is the gap, and the gap becomes the action plan.

Look at what a Profile contains: a requirement (the Subcategory), a statement of the actual situation (evidence), a comparison (gap) and an action. That is exactly the structure of a conformity assessment, which is why we call a Profile a small conformity assessment. In the Project, your Target Profile for the five critical assets is the reference against which Sections 6 and 7 are written.

NIST also publishes Community Profiles (shared Target Profiles for a sector or a technology) and free Quick-Start Guides, including the Small Business Quick-Start Guide (NIST SP (Special Publication) 1300), which is the recommended entry point for a company of Érable Cycles’ size. The Informative References connect each Subcategory to detailed sources — NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 controls, CIS Controls Safeguards, ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission) 27001 controls — through the NIST OLIR (Online Informative References) program and the CPRT (Cybersecurity and Privacy Reference Tool) online tool. We use them in Lesson 5 as crosswalks.

1.5 What the CSF gives Érable Cycles — and what it does not

  • Gives: a common vocabulary with the CEO (chief executive officer) and the MSP (six verbs everybody understands), a structure for the Target Profile, free mappings to the detailed frameworks, and a way to show progress year after year (Current Profile 2025 vs 2026).
  • Does not give: configuration settings (no password length, no firewall rule), a certification (nobody is “CSF-certified”), or a legal obligation (the law is PIPEDA (Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act), Law 25, GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation), CASL (Canada’s Anti-Spam Legislation); the contract is PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard)). The CSF organizes the work; it does not replace the requirements.

Hence the default framework pair proposed in Lab 1: CIS Controls v8.1 IG1 (Implementation Group 1) for the concrete safeguards and a CSF 2.0 Profile for the structure and the reporting.

Key terms of this lesson

FrameworkA structured set of outcomes or practices an organization chooses to follow; voluntary unless a law or a contract makes it mandatory.
Function / Category / SubcategoryThe three levels of the CSF (Cybersecurity Framework) Core: broad outcome → group of outcomes → one specific, testable outcome.
Govern (GV)The sixth Function added in CSF 2.0: strategy, expectations, policy, roles, oversight, supply-chain risk.
TierOne of four descriptions (Partial, Risk Informed, Repeatable, Adaptive) of how rigorously cybersecurity risk is governed and managed — not a maturity ranking.
Current Profile / Target ProfileThe outcomes achieved today / the outcomes wanted; the difference is the gap and feeds the action plan.
Informative ReferenceA mapping from a CSF Subcategory to a detailed source (SP (Special Publication) 800-53, CIS (Center for Internet Security) Controls, ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission) 27001) — the basis of crosswalks.

Real-life example — A Current vs Target Profile for Érable Cycles in seven lines

Task of this example: Build a very small Organizational Profile: one Subcategory per Function (plus one extra for Protect), score the current state and the target on a 0–4 scale, compute the gap and rank the gaps so that the largest ones become the first actions of the audit plan.
Relation to the lecture: Applies sections 1.2 and 1.4: the Subcategory identifiers, the Current / Target Profile and the gap. It shows why a Profile is a conformity assessment in miniature.
Part of future labs:Lab 1 — Part B.1 — the justification of the framework choice (‘a CSF Profile gives the structure, IG1 gives the safeguards’) and the Target Profile that appears in Project Section 5Lab 2 — the assessment plan schedules the checks of the Subcategories with the largest gaps firstProject — Section 7 — the risk rating of non-conformities uses the same gaps

The CEO (chief executive officer) of Érable Cycles asks the audit team for “a one-page view of where we stand”. The team picks seven Subcategories that match the company’s obligations and risks, interviews the IT (information technology) administrator and scores each one twice: current (what the evidence shows today) and target (what the laws, PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) and the CEO’s risk appetite require by next year). Scale used by the team: 0 = not performed, 1 = informal, 2 = partially documented, 3 = documented and applied, 4 = applied and measured. The scale is the team’s own; the CSF (Cybersecurity Framework) does not impose one.

Deliverables of the example:
  • A Profile table with seven rows (Subcategory · Function · current · target · gap)
  • A ranked gap list: the three largest gaps become the first checks of the Lab 2 plan
  • One bar chart, current vs target per Function, for the executive summary

Code illustration — L1_csf_profile_gap.py (Python 3)

Task of the code: Read the seven-row Profile from L1_csf_profile.csv, compute the gap of every Subcategory, print the Profile table, rank the gaps and write a ranked CSV for the assessment plan.
Relation to the lecture: Illustrates section 1.4: Current Profile, Target Profile and gap. Each row of the CSV is one Subcategory; the script does what an analyst does with a highlighter — it finds the largest distances between ‘is’ and ‘should be’.
Run it: python3 L1_csf_profile_gap.py · data file: L1_csf_profile.csv
L1_csf_profile_gap.py 
1# Import the csv module from the standard library: it reads and writes comma-separated files safely (quotes, commas inside text).2import csv3# The input file: one line per Subcategory with the columns id, function, outcome, current, target.4INPUT = "L1_csf_profile.csv"5# The output file: the same rows sorted by gap, which the Lab 2 plan uses to order the checks.6OUTPUT = "L1_csf_gaps_ranked.csv"7# Open the input file for reading; newline='' is required by the csv module; utf-8 keeps the accented characters of the outcome texts.8with open(INPUT, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:9#     DictReader returns each row as a dictionary keyed by the header names, so we can write row['current'] instead of row[3].10    rows = list(csv.DictReader(f))11# Loop over every Subcategory row; this is where the Profile logic happens.12for row in rows:13#     Convert the two scores from text to integers; CSV files only contain text.14    current, target = int(row["current"]), int(row["target"])15#     The gap is simply target minus current; a positive gap means work is needed, zero means the outcome is already at the target.16    row["gap"] = target - current17# Sort the rows by gap, largest first (reverse=True); ties keep the original order, so the Govern row stays first among equals.18ranked = sorted(rows, key=lambda r: r["gap"], reverse=True)19# Print a header for the Profile table; the format string pads each column so the output lines up.20print(f"{'Subcategory':<10} {'Function':<9} {'Cur':>3} {'Tgt':>3} {'Gap':>3}")21# Print one line per Subcategory in ranked order.22for r in ranked:23#     Each value is taken from the dictionary; the > and < signs align numbers right and text left.24    print(f"{r['id']:<10} {r['function']:<9} {r['current']:>3} {r['target']:>3} {r['gap']:>3}")25# Compute the total gap of the Profile: the sum of all individual gaps, one number for the executive summary.26total_gap = sum(r["gap"] for r in ranked)27# Compute the maximum possible gap (every row at 0 with target 4) to express the total as a percentage.28print(f"Total gap: {total_gap} points over {len(ranked)} Subcategories")29# Open the output file for writing; the plan of Lab 2 reads this file to schedule the checks.30with open(OUTPUT, "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:31#     DictWriter writes dictionaries as rows; fieldnames fixes the column order, gap included.32    w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=["id", "function", "outcome", "current", "target", "gap"])33#     Write the header line first.34    w.writeheader()35#     Then write every ranked row.36    w.writerows(ranked)37# Tell the user where the ranked list is; the three first rows become the first checks of the audit plan.38print(f"Ranked gaps written to {OUTPUT}; top-3 checks: " + ", ".join(r['id'] for r in ranked[:3]))
Execution steps — click a step to jump to it; pause to discuss
    Variables at this step: 
    
  
    
 
    
 
    

    

    Step-by-step explanation
    1. The script reads a small table, one Subcategory per line, with the current and target scores given by the audit team.
    2. For every line it computes gap = target − current. This single subtraction is the whole idea of a Profile: the distance between the situation observed and the situation required.
    3. It sorts the lines by gap, largest first, because an audit plan tests the largest distances first — they are the most likely non-conformities and the biggest risks.
    4. It prints the Profile table and the total gap (one number the CEO can follow year after year), then writes the ranked list to a CSV file that the Lab 2 assessment plan uses as its ordered list of checks.
    5. The visualization shows, for each Function, the current score (dark bar) and the target score (light bar). The visible space between the two bars is the gap you just computed.

    ISO/IEC 27001:2022 — the ISMS standard and its 93 Annex A controls
    ≈ 10 min · Lesson 2 of 6
    

    Learning objectives — after this lesson you can:
    • Describe what ISO/IEC 27001 certifies (a management system, not a product).
    • Name the clauses 4–10 and the four themes of Annex A with their control counts.
    • Explain the Statement of Applicability and why control A.5.31 is the control behind Lab 1.
    • Place ISO/IEC 27002, internal audit (9.2) and management review (9.3) in the picture.
    2.1 What ISO/IEC 27001 is
    

    ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission) 27001:2022 is the international standard that specifies the requirements of an information security management system (ISMS): the set of policies, processes, roles and records through which an organization manages its information security risks. It is published jointly by the ISO (International Organization for Standardization) and the IEC (International Electrotechnical Commission). The current (third) edition was published on October 25, 2022; Amendment 1 (February 2024) added climate-change considerations to clauses 4.1 and 4.2. Organizations certified against the 2013 edition had until October 31, 2025 to transition, so every valid certificate today refers to the 2022 edition.
    

    Two things distinguish ISO/IEC 27001 from the CSF (Cybersecurity Framework) of Lesson 1. First, it is certifiable: an accredited certification body audits the organization and issues a certificate valid three years, with surveillance audits every year. In Canada, certification bodies are accredited by the Standards Council of Canada (SCC); other national accreditation bodies play the same role elsewhere (ANAB in the United States, UKAS in the United Kingdom). Second, it is a licensed text: the standard must be purchased from ISO or a national member body and may not be copied or redistributed (Legal Notice, section 7.5). In this course we cite clause and control numbers only.
    2.2 Clauses 4 to 10 — the management system
    

    Clauses 1–3 are scope, references and definitions. The requirements are in clauses 4 to 10 and follow the PDCA (Plan-Do-Check-Act) cycle you met on Day 1:
    

    ClauseTitleWhat the auditor looks for
    

    4Context of the organizationInterested parties, their requirements (laws, contracts), the scope of the ISMS
    

    5LeadershipManagement commitment, the information security policy, roles and responsibilities
    

    6PlanningRisk assessment and risk treatment; 6.1.3 d) requires the Statement of Applicability; security objectives
    

    7SupportResources, competence, awareness, communication, 7.5 documented information (Lesson 6)
    

    8OperationThe plans are executed; risk assessments repeated at planned intervals
    

    9Performance evaluation9.1 monitoring and measurement, 9.2 internal audit, 9.3 management review
    

    10Improvement10.1 continual improvement, 10.2 nonconformity and corrective action
    

    

    Clause 9.2 is the reason this course exists: every certified organization must run internal audits at planned intervals, by competent and impartial auditors, and report the results to management. Clause 10.2 defines the nonconformity → corrective action → verification loop that your Project Sections 7 and 8 reproduce.
    2.3 Annex A — 93 controls in four themes
    

    Annex A is a reference list of 93 information security controls grouped in four themes: 5 Organizational (37 controls), 6 People (8), 7 Physical (14) and 8 Technological (34). The 2013 edition had 114 controls in 14 domains; the 2022 edition merged many of them and added 11 new controls, among them 5.7 Threat intelligence, 5.23 Information security for use of cloud services, 8.9 Configuration management, 8.10 Information deletion, 8.12 Data leakage prevention, 8.16 Monitoring activities and 8.28 Secure coding.
    

    Annex A is not optional reading: clause 6.1.3 requires the organization to compare its chosen risk treatments with Annex A to make sure no necessary control was forgotten, and to record the result in the Statement of Applicability (SoA) — the list of all 93 controls with, for each one, applicable or not, the justification, and whether it is implemented. The SoA is the first document an ISO auditor asks for, and the example below builds an extract of it.
    

    Controls you will meet again in this course:
    

      

    • A.5.31 Legal, statutory, regulatory and contractual requirements — identify, document and keep up to date the requirements that apply. This is the control behind Lab 1.
      • 

    • A.5.34 Privacy and protection of PII — the control that carries PIPEDA (Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act), Law 25 and the GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) inside the ISMS.
      • 

    • A.5.9 Inventory of information and other associated assets, A.5.12 Classification — Lab 2.
      • 

    • A.5.33 Protection of records — retention and disposal (Lesson 4).
      • 

    • A.5.37 Documented operating procedures — your Course Procedure Manual is exactly this control applied to the audit.
      • 

    • A.8.8 Management of technical vulnerabilities, A.8.9 Configuration management, A.8.15 Logging, A.5.15 Access control, A.5.18 Access rights — Lab 3.
      • 

    2.4 ISO/IEC 27002 and the control attributes
    

    ISO/IEC 27002:2022 is the companion guidance document: for each of the 93 controls it gives the purpose, implementation guidance and five attributes (control type: preventive / detective / corrective; information security properties: confidentiality / integrity / availability; cybersecurity concepts: Identify / Protect / Detect / Respond / Recover — the CSF Functions; operational capabilities; security domains). The attributes are a built-in crosswalk to the CSF, which we use in Lesson 5.
    

    Other members of the family worth knowing by name: ISO/IEC 27005 (risk management guidance), ISO/IEC 27701 (privacy information management, extension for PIPEDA/GDPR-type obligations) and ISO 19011 (auditing management systems — the audit principles of Day 1).
    2.5 When does an SME choose ISO/IEC 27001?
    

    Certification costs time (12–18 months of implementation for a first certificate is common), money (consultants, certification body fees) and ongoing effort (annual surveillance). An SME (small or medium-sized enterprise) chooses it when a customer, a partner or a tender requires the certificate, when it wants to sell into markets where the certificate is expected, or when it needs an externally verified signal of trust. Érable Cycles has none of these drivers today, which is why the default in Lab 1 is CIS (Center for Internet Security) IG1 (Implementation Group 1) + a CSF Profile — and why ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A remains the documented alternative if a student argues, for example, that the AWS (Amazon Web Services) web store will be sold to corporate fleets that demand it.
    Key terms of this lesson
    ISMSInformation security management system: the policies, processes, roles and records through which an organization manages its information security risks.
    Certification bodyAn independent organization, accredited by a national body (SCC (Standards Council of Canada) in Canada), that audits an ISMS (information security management system) against ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission) 27001 and issues the certificate.
    Statement of Applicability (SoA)The list of all 93 Annex A controls with applicable / not applicable, justification and implementation status (clause 6.1.3 d)).
    Annex A themeOne of the four groups of controls: Organizational (37), People (8), Physical (14), Technological (34).
    Internal audit (9.2)Planned, impartial audit of the ISMS by the organization’s own (or contracted) auditors; results reported to management.
    Nonconformity (10.2)A failure to fulfil a requirement; triggers correction, root-cause analysis, corrective action and verification.

    Real-life example — A Statement of Applicability extract for Érable Cycles
    

    Task of this example: Take twelve Annex A controls that matter for the company, decide for each one whether it is applicable (with a one-line justification), record whether it is implemented today, then count the result per theme and list the controls that are applicable but not implemented — they are the candidate findings of the audit.
    Relation to the lecture: Applies sections 2.3 and 2.5: Annex A themes, the SoA as the list of applicable controls with justification, and the idea that an applicable-but-missing control is a nonconformity candidate (clause 10.2).
    

    Part of future labs:Lab 1 — Part B.1 — the justification text if the ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A alternative is chosen; the SoA extract is attached to Project Section 5Lab 2 — the audit checklist maps each item to an Annex A control number (ISO column of the Master Checklist)Lab 3 — A.8.9 configuration management and A.8.15 logging are tested with CIS-CAT Lite, Lynis and the check scripts
    

    A corporate customer asks Érable Cycles whether it is “ISO (International Organization for Standardization) 27001 ready”. Instead of answering yes or no, the IT (information technology) administrator and the audit team fill a twelve-row extract of a Statement of Applicability: for each control they note the theme, whether it applies (a control about software development, A.8.28 Secure coding, does not — the web store is a packaged product maintained by the MSP (managed service provider)), why, and whether it is in place today. The result shows the customer where the company stands and gives the audit team its first list of gaps.
    Deliverables of the example:
    • A 12-row SoA extract: control · theme · applicable (Y/N) · justification · implemented (Y/N)
    • Counts per theme: applicable and implemented
    • The list of applicable-but-not-implemented controls = candidate findings for Lab 3 and Project Section 7

    Task of the code: Read L2_soa_extract.csv (12 Annex A controls), print the SoA extract as a table, count applicable and implemented controls per theme, and list the applicable controls that are not implemented.
    Relation to the lecture: Illustrates section 2.3: the Statement of Applicability. The script is the ‘counting and filtering’ an auditor does on the SoA before the first interview.
    Run it: bash L2_soa_extract.sh · data file: L2_soa_extract.csv
    

    
 
    L2_soa_extract.sh
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
    
 
    
  
    1# Tell the system to run this file with Bash, the default shell of the Ubuntu VM.2#!/usr/bin/env bash3# Stop at the first error (-e), treat unset variables as errors (-u) and fail a pipeline if any command in it fails (-o pipefail).4set -euo pipefail5# Name of the input file: one line per control, columns control;theme;applicable;justification;implemented (semicolon-separated so that commas can appear in the justification).6INPUT="L2_soa_extract.csv"7# Print the table header; printf gives fixed column widths so the output is readable in the evidence screenshot.8printf "%-7s %-14s %-4s %-4s %s\n" "Control" "Theme" "App" "Impl" "Justification"9# Read the file line by line; IFS=';' splits each line at semicolons into the five variables; tail -n +2 skips the header line.10while IFS=';' read -r ctrl theme app just impl; do11#     Print one formatted row per control.12  printf "%-7s %-14s %-4s %-4s %s\n" "$ctrl" "$theme" "$app" "$impl" "$just"13# End of the loop; the input redirection feeds the loop with the file minus its header.14done < <(tail -n +2 "$INPUT")15# Print a blank line and a sub-title before the counts.16printf "\nApplicable / implemented per theme\n"17# awk processes the file again: -F';' sets the separator; NR>1 skips the header; for each line it adds 1 to the counters of the theme.18awk -F';' 'NR>1 { total[$2]++; if ($3=="Y") app[$2]++; if ($3=="Y" && $5=="Y") impl[$2]++ }19#     At the end (END block) awk prints one line per theme: total controls listed, applicable, implemented.20     END { for (t in total) printf "%-14s listed=%d applicable=%d implemented=%d\n", t, total[t], app[t]+0, impl[t]+0 }' "$INPUT"21# Sub-title for the gap list.22printf "\nApplicable but NOT implemented (candidate findings)\n"23# awk filters the lines where applicable is Y and implemented is N and prints the control number and its justification.24awk -F';' 'NR>1 && $3=="Y" && $5=="N" { printf "  %s — %s\n", $1, $4 }' "$INPUT"25# Count the gaps with grep -c (count matching lines) on the same filter, to give one number for the summary; || true keeps the script alive if the count is zero.26GAPS=$(awk -F';' 'NR>1 && $3=="Y" && $5=="N"' "$INPUT" | wc -l || true)27# Final one-line summary used in the lab write-up.28printf "\n%s applicable control(s) not implemented → to be tested in Lab 3\n" "$GAPS"

      Step-by-step explanation
      1. The CSV holds twelve Annex A controls with the five SoA columns. Semicolons separate the columns because justifications contain commas.
      2. The while read loop prints the extract as a table — this is the document the customer and the auditor read.
      3. The first awk command counts, per theme, how many controls are listed, how many apply and how many of the applicable ones are implemented. awk is the standard Linux tool for column arithmetic on text files.
      4. The second awk command filters the rows that are applicable but not implemented. Each of them is a candidate nonconformity (clause 10.2) that Lab 3 will test with evidence.
      5. The visualization is the SoA table itself: rows fill in one by one; green = applicable and implemented, red = applicable but not implemented, grey = not applicable (with a justification, as the SoA requires).

      3
      CIS Critical Security Controls v8.1 — Controls, Safeguards, Implementation Groups; Controls vs Benchmarks; choosing for an SME
      ≈ 9 min · Lesson 3 of 6
      

      Learning objectives — after this lesson you can:
      • Describe the structure of the CIS Controls v8.1: 18 Controls, 153 Safeguards, three Implementation Groups.
      • Explain why IG1 is the starting point for an SME.
      • Distinguish CIS Controls (program level) from CIS Benchmarks (product configuration) — the distinction Lab 3 relies on.
      • Choose a framework set for Érable Cycles and justify it in three sentences (Lab 1 Part B.1).
      3.1 What the CIS Controls are
      

      The CIS (Center for Internet Security) Critical Security Controls are a prioritized set of defensive actions published by the Center for Internet Security (CIS), a non-profit organization. Version 8 was released in May 2021; version 8.1 (June 2024) added a Governance security function, aligned the vocabulary with the CSF (Cybersecurity Framework) 2.0 and clarified asset classes, without adding or removing any Safeguard. The document is free (registration on the CIS site).
      

      The structure has three levels. A Control is a broad area of defence (18 of them). A Safeguard is one specific, measurable action inside a Control (153 in total; they were called sub-controls before version 8). An Implementation Group (IG) is a subset of Safeguards recommended for a type of organization. Unlike the CSF, which states outcomes, a Safeguard says what to do: for example Safeguard 4.1 “Establish and maintain a secure configuration process” or Safeguard 5.2 “Use unique passwords”.
      3.2 The 18 Controls
      

      #ControlIG1 (Implementation Group 1) Safeguards#ControlIG1 Safeguards
      

      1Inventory and Control of Enterprise Assets210Malware Defenses3
      

      2Inventory and Control of Software Assets311Data Recovery4
      

      3Data Protection612Network Infrastructure Management1
      

      4Secure Configuration of Enterprise Assets and Software713Network Monitoring and Defense0
      

      5Account Management414Security Awareness and Skills Training8
      

      6Access Control Management515Service Provider Management1
      

      7Continuous Vulnerability Management416Application Software Security0
      

      8Audit Log Management317Incident Response Management3
      

      9Email and Web Browser Protections218Penetration Testing0
      

      

      The Controls are ordered: 1 and 2 (inventories) come first because you cannot protect what you do not know you have — which is exactly why Lab 2 inventories the assets before any technical test. Controls 4, 5, 6, 8 and 12 are the ones Lab 3 tests on the two VMs (virtual machines).
      3.3 Implementation Groups: IG1 = essential cyber hygiene
      

      IG1 contains 56 Safeguards and is defined by CIS as essential cyber hygiene: the minimum standard of information security for every enterprise, designed for organizations with limited IT (information technology) and security expertise whose main concern is to keep operating. IG2 (Implementation Group 2) adds 74 Safeguards (130 in total) for organizations with dedicated IT staff that manage sensitive information; IG3 (Implementation Group 3) adds the last 23 (153) for organizations facing targeted attacks or regulatory scrutiny. The groups are cumulative: IG2 includes all of IG1, IG3 includes all of IG2.
      

      Three Controls have no IG1 Safeguard at all — 13 Network Monitoring and Defense, 16 Application Software Security and 18 Penetration Testing — which tells an SME (small or medium-sized enterprise) what it may postpone without being negligent. CIS’s Community Defense Model analysis, based on the MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques and Common Knowledge) knowledge base, reports that IG1 alone defends against a large majority of the most common attack techniques, which is the evidence-based argument for starting there. With 45 employees, one IT administrator and an MSP (managed service provider), Érable Cycles is a textbook IG1 organization.
      3.4 CIS Controls versus CIS Benchmarks — the distinction Lab 3 relies on
      

      CIS publishes two different families of documents and students mix them up constantly:
      

      CIS ControlsCIS Benchmarks
      

      LevelProgram — what an organization should doProduct — how one technology should be configured
      

      Unit18 Controls, 153 SafeguardsMore than 100 Benchmarks (Windows 11, Ubuntu, Google Chrome, AWS (Amazon Web Services), Microsoft 365…), each with hundreds of recommendations
      

      ProfilesIG1, IG2, IG3Level 1 (essential, low impact) and Level 2 (defence in depth)
      

      ExampleSafeguard 4.1 Establish and maintain a secure configuration processWindows 11 Benchmark: “Interactive logon: Machine inactivity limit” ≤ 900 seconds
      

      Assessed withCIS CSAT (self-assessment), interviews, document reviewCIS-CAT (CIS Configuration Assessment Tool) Lite (Lab 3), Policy Analyzer, Lynis (own tests)
      

      In this courseLab 1 (framework choice), Lab 2 (checklist items)Lab 3 (configuration audit of the Windows and Ubuntu VMs)
      

      

      The link between the two: Safeguard 4.1 asks for a secure configuration process; the Benchmark is the concrete standard that process applies. When CIS-CAT Lite reports 71 % on the Windows 11 Enterprise Benchmark Level 1, you are measuring conformity to the Benchmark and using it as evidence for Safeguard 4.1.
      3.5 Mappings and tools around the Controls
      

        

      • Mappings (free): CIS Controls v8.1 ↔ NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) CSF 2.0, ↔ ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission) 27001:2022, ↔ PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) v4.0, ↔ NIST SP (Special Publication) 800-53 Rev. 5 — downloadable spreadsheets and the online CIS Controls Navigator. They are the crosswalks of Lesson 5.
        • 

      • CIS CSAT (Controls Self Assessment Tool, free hosted version): score each Safeguard’s policy, implementation, automation and reporting; produces the IG1 coverage figure the example computes by hand.
        • 

      • CIS RAM (Risk Assessment Method) (Risk Assessment Method): a risk method aligned with the Controls — mention only; this course uses a 3×3 matrix (Lab 2).
        • 

      3.6 Choosing for an SME — the three-sentence justification
      

      Lab 1 Part B.1 asks you to pick two frameworks and justify the choice in three sentences. Use this decision logic:
      

        

      1. PCI DSS is not a choice. Whenever payment cards are accepted, PCI DSS applies by contract whatever else is chosen; the only decision is the scope (hosted payment page + P2PE (point-to-point encryption) terminals → SAQ (Self-Assessment Questionnaire) A-type validation for the web store and SAQ P2PE for the stores).
        2. 

      2. Start with CIS Controls v8.1 IG1 for the concrete safeguards: 56 actions, free, prioritized, with Benchmarks and CIS-CAT for the technical tests, and official mappings to everything else.
        3. 

      3. Add a NIST CSF 2.0 Organizational Profile for structure and reporting: the six Functions organize the report to the CEO (chief executive officer) and the Target Profile shows progress year after year.
        4. 

      4. Move to ISO/IEC 27001 only when a customer, a partner or a market requires the certificate — then Annex A becomes the reference and the SoA (Statement of Applicability) the key document.
        5. 

      

      Example of an acceptable justification: “Érable Cycles has 45 employees, one IT administrator and no customer requiring certification, so a free, prioritized list of safeguards is the practical reference: CIS Controls v8.1 IG1. A NIST CSF 2.0 Profile structures the report to the CEO and lets us compare this year with last year’s six results. PCI DSS v4.0.1 applies in any case through the merchant agreement, with a reduced scope thanks to the hosted payment page and the P2PE terminals.”
      Key terms of this lesson
      Control (CIS)One of 18 broad areas of defence in the CIS (Center for Internet Security) Critical Security Controls.
      SafeguardOne specific, measurable action inside a Control (153 in v8.1; formerly ‘sub-control’).
      Implementation Group (IG)A cumulative subset of Safeguards recommended for a type of organization: IG1 (56), IG2 (130), IG3 (153).
      Essential cyber hygieneCIS’s name for IG1: the minimum standard of information security for every enterprise.
      CIS BenchmarkA per-product configuration standard (Windows 11, Ubuntu, Chrome, AWS (Amazon Web Services)…) with Level 1 / Level 2 profiles, assessed with CIS-CAT (CIS Configuration Assessment Tool).
      Crosswalk / mappingA table that links the items of one framework to the equivalent items of another (CIS ↔ CSF (Cybersecurity Framework) ↔ ISO (International Organization for Standardization) ↔ PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard)).

      Real-life example — IG1 coverage of Érable Cycles in fourteen Safeguards
      

      Task of this example: Score fourteen IG1 Safeguards that matter for the company (Implemented / Partial / Missing), compute the coverage per Control and overall, and separate the Safeguards that are verified at program level (documents, interviews) from the ones whose evidence comes from a Benchmark assessment on the VMs in Lab 3.
      Relation to the lecture: Applies sections 3.3 and 3.4: IG1 as the SME reference and the Controls-versus-Benchmarks distinction. The coverage figure is what CIS CSAT would produce; the ‘evidence source’ column is the bridge to Lab 3.
      

      Part of future labs:Lab 1 — Part B.1 — the justification of CIS IG1 as the primary framework and the coverage figure quoted in Project Section 5Lab 2 — the 12–15 checklist items are taken from exactly these IG1 SafeguardsLab 3 — the Safeguards marked ‘Benchmark’ are tested with CIS-CAT Lite, Policy Analyzer and Lynis; the ‘Program’ ones with the 5-question policy check
      

      Before writing the assessment plan, the audit team asks the IT (information technology) administrator fourteen yes / partly / no questions taken from IG1 (Implementation Group 1) — one or two per Control that applies to the company. Each answer is scored 1, 0.5 or 0. The team also notes where the proof will come from: a document or an interview (Program), or a configuration check on a system (Benchmark). The coverage per Control tells the CEO (chief executive officer) where the company is weakest; the evidence column tells the team which checks belong in Lab 3.
      Deliverables of the example:
      • A 14-row IG1 scorecard: Safeguard · Control · status · score · evidence source
      • Coverage per Control and overall (percent)
      • Two lists: Program-level checks (policy review) and Benchmark-level checks (Lab 3 tools)
      


      Code illustration — L3_cis_ig1_coverage.ps1 (PowerShell 7)
      

      Task of the code: Read L3_cis_ig1_sample.csv (14 IG1 Safeguards with a status and an evidence source), convert the status to a score, compute the coverage per Control and overall, and list which Safeguards are verified by documents (Program) and which by a Benchmark assessment on a VM.
      Relation to the lecture: Illustrates sections 3.3 and 3.4: IG1 coverage (what CIS CSAT measures) and the Controls-versus-Benchmarks distinction (where the evidence comes from).
      Run it: pwsh -File L3_cis_ig1_coverage.ps1  (or run in Windows PowerShell 5.1) · data file: L3_cis_ig1_sample.csv
      

      
 
      L3_cis_ig1_coverage.ps1
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
      
 
      
  
      1# Import-Csv reads the file and returns one object per line, with a property for every column (Safeguard, Control, Title, Status, Evidence).2$rows = Import-Csv -Path "L3_cis_ig1_sample.csv"3# A hashtable that converts the three possible statuses into a numeric score; Partial counts as half a Safeguard.4$score = @{ Implemented = 1.0; Partial = 0.5; Missing = 0.0 }5# Loop over every Safeguard; the pipeline sends each object to the script block as $_ .6$rows | ForEach-Object {7#     Add a calculated property Score to the object by looking the status up in the hashtable.8    $_ | Add-Member -NotePropertyName Score -NotePropertyValue $score[$_.Status]9# End of the first loop; every row now carries its score.10}11# Print the scorecard as a table: the five columns the lab write-up needs; Out-String renders the table as text so it also prints when the script is run from a file.12$rows | Format-Table Safeguard, Control, Status, Score, Evidence -AutoSize | Out-String -Width 12013# Group the rows by Control number so that the coverage can be computed per Control.14$byControl = $rows | Group-Object Control15# For every group, compute the average score of its Safeguards and express it as a percentage.16$coverage = foreach ($g in $byControl) {17#     Measure-Object -Average returns the mean of the Score property; [math]::Round keeps whole percents.18    $avg = ($g.Group | Measure-Object -Property Score -Average).Average19#     Build a small output object per Control with the number of Safeguards checked and the coverage.20    [pscustomobject]@{ Control = [int]$g.Name; Safeguards = $g.Count; Coverage = [int][math]::Round($avg * 100) }21# End of the per-Control loop.22}23# Print the coverage per Control, sorted by Control number, as a table (Out-String again renders it as text).24$coverage | Sort-Object Control | Format-Table -AutoSize | Out-String -Width 12025# Overall coverage: the sum of all scores divided by the number of Safeguards checked, as a percentage.26$overall = [math]::Round((($rows | Measure-Object -Property Score -Sum).Sum / $rows.Count) * 100)27# Print the single number the CEO asks for.28Write-Output ("Overall IG1 coverage on the 14 Safeguards checked: {0}%" -f $overall)29# Filter the Safeguards whose evidence comes from a Benchmark assessment on a VM: these are the Lab 3 tool checks.30$bench = $rows | Where-Object { $_.Evidence -eq "Benchmark" }31# Filter the Safeguards verified with documents and interviews: these are policy checks (Program level).32$prog  = $rows | Where-Object { $_.Evidence -eq "Program" }33# Print both lists on one line each, Safeguard numbers joined with commas.34Write-Output ("Benchmark checks (Lab 3 tools): " + (($bench.Safeguard) -join ", "))35# The Program list closes the report.36Write-Output ("Program checks (documents, interviews): " + (($prog.Safeguard) -join ", "))

        Step-by-step explanation
        1. The CSV lists fourteen IG1 Safeguards with the administrator’s answer (Implemented, Partial, Missing) and the type of evidence that will prove it (Program or Benchmark).
        2. A hashtable turns the answers into numbers: 1, 0.5, 0. Scoring Partial as 0.5 is a convention the team writes in its plan; CIS CSAT uses finer scales.
        3. Group-Object Control gathers the Safeguards of the same Control; the average score of each group, multiplied by 100, is the coverage of that Control.
        4. The overall coverage is the mean of all fourteen scores — a single figure for the executive summary, to be compared with next year’s.
        5. Two Where-Object filters split the Safeguards by evidence source. The Benchmark ones (secure configuration, firewall, logging, patching) are tested with CIS-CAT Lite, Policy Analyzer and Lynis in Lab 3; the Program ones (inventory process, training, incident contacts) are tested with the five-question document check.
        6. The visualization draws one bar per Control; the bar fills as its Safeguards are scored, so the weakest Controls are visible at a glance.

        4
        Data retention policies — legal minimums, legal maximums and the retention schedule
        ≈ 8 min · Lesson 4 of 6
        

        Learning objectives — after this lesson you can:
        • Distinguish a legal minimum retention period (keep at least) from a legal maximum (keep no longer than necessary).
        • Cite the sources that set each one for Érable Cycles: CRA and Revenu Québec, PIPEDA 4.5, Law 25 section 23, GDPR Article 5(1)(e), PCI DSS 3.2.1 and 10.5.1.
        • Fill the seven columns of a retention schedule for a record type.
        • Recognize the two retention non-conformities: deleting too early and keeping too long.
        4.1 Two forces pull in opposite directions
        

        A retention period is the length of time a record is kept before it is destroyed or anonymized. Two kinds of rules decide it. A legal minimum says “keep at least this long”: tax and accounting law, and some security standards, need the record to exist for later verification. A legal maximum says “keep no longer than necessary for the purpose”: the privacy laws apply it to every record that contains personal information (PI). A record can be subject to both at the same time — an invoice contains the customer’s name and address (privacy maximum) and is a tax record (six-year minimum). When the two conflict, the legal minimum wins for as long as it lasts, because the privacy laws themselves make an exception for retention periods fixed by another law; after that, the maximum applies and the record must go.
        

        A data retention policy states the rules; a retention schedule applies them record type by record type. Both are required or expected by the texts of Day 2: PIPEDA (Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act) Principle 4.5.2 asks for guidelines and procedures with minimum and maximum retention periods; Law 25 section 3.2 requires governance policies that provide a framework for the keeping and destruction of personal information; the GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) asks organizations to tell individuals how long data is kept (Article 13(2)(a)) and to record the envisaged time limits for erasure in the record of processing (Article 30); PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) requirement 3.2.1 requires a data retention and disposal policy for account data.
        4.2 The sources, text by text
        

        SourceRuleMinimum or maximum?Applies at Érable Cycles to
        

        CRA (Canada Revenue Agency) (Income Tax Act, Excise Tax Act) and Revenu QuébecKeep records and supporting documents six years from the end of the last tax year they relate toMinimumOrders, invoices, payment records, payroll
        

        PIPEDA Principle 4.5 (Schedule 1)Retain PI only as long as necessary for the purposes; 4.5.2 guidelines with minimum and maximum periods; 4.5.3 destroy, erase or anonymizeMaximumCustomer accounts, newsletter list, CCTV (closed-circuit television), logs with identifiers
        

        PIPEDA Breach Regulations (SOR/2018-64) s. 6Keep a record of every breach of security safeguards for 24 monthsMinimumThe breach register
        

        Law 25 — Private Sector Act s. 23When the purposes are achieved, destroy or anonymize the information, subject to any preservation period provided by law (anonymization follows the 2024 regulation)MaximumSame records as PIPEDA, for Québec
        

        Law 25 — confidentiality-incident regulationKeep the incident register entries five years after the organization becomes aware of the incidentMinimumThe incident register
        

        GDPR Article 5(1)(e) — storage limitationKeep personal data in identifiable form no longer than necessary; inform individuals of the period or the criteria (Art. 13); record time limits in the ROPA (Art. 30)MaximumData of customers located in the EU (European Union)
        

        PCI DSS v4.0.1 requirement 3.2.1Account data storage kept to a minimum: retention and disposal policy, retention limited to legal / regulatory / business need, secure deletion, and a check at least once every three months that data past its period is goneMaximum (with a verification duty)Any cardholder data — Érable Cycles stores none, and must prove it
        

        PCI DSS v4.0.1 requirement 10.5.1Keep audit log history at least 12 months, with the most recent three months immediately available for analysisMinimumLogs of systems in or connected to the CDE (cardholder data environment); the course uses it as the reference for all server and firewall logs
        

        CASL (Canada’s Anti-Spam Legislation) (s. 13; CRTC (Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission) guidance)The sender must be able to prove consent; proceedings can start up to three years after the CRTC learns of a violationMinimum (in practice)Newsletter consent records
        

        CCTV — OPC (Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada) and CAI (Commission d’accès à l’information du Québec) guidanceNo fixed statutory period; keep recordings only as long as necessary and destroy them quickly unless needed for an incidentMaximumStore cameras
        

        

        One more rule worth knowing: PIPEDA requires that personal information used to make a decision about a person be kept long enough for that person to access it afterwards — so “delete immediately” is also wrong for records such as a refused refund.
        4.3 The seven columns of a retention schedule
        

        A usable schedule has one line per record type and seven columns:
        

          

        1. Record type — and whether it contains personal information (Y/N (yes / no)) and cardholder data (Y/N).
          2. 

        2. Legal basis — the minimum rule and the maximum rule that apply (article numbers).
          3. 

        3. Retention period — the number chosen, which must be ≥ the minimum and justified against the maximum.
          4. 

        4. Trigger — the event that starts the clock: end of the tax year, closing of the account, last activity, date of the recording.
          5. 

        5. Disposal method — secure deletion, anonymization, shredding; who confirms it.
          6. 

        6. Owner — the business role accountable (not the IT (information technology) custodian).
          7. 

        7. Exceptions — legal hold: when a dispute, a complaint or an investigation is reasonably anticipated, destruction is suspended for the records concerned.
          8. 

        

        Two non-conformities come out of a schedule check: destroyed too early (below a legal minimum — tax records shredded after three years, logs rotated after 30 days when 12 months are required) and kept too long (past the purpose without a legal basis — a newsletter list with addresses collected ten years ago, CCTV kept for a year). Lab 3 finds the second kind on the VMs (log rotation settings) and the first kind in the policies.
        4.4 Retention and the audit tools
        

        Retention is tested with documents and with configuration: the Ubuntu VM (virtual machine)’s /etc/logrotate.conf and journald settings, the Windows event-log maximum sizes, the backup NAS (network-attached storage) retention and the Microsoft 365 retention policies (Purview Data Lifecycle Management — instructor demo). A policy that says “12 months” and a server that overwrites its logs after 2 weeks is a non-conformity with evidence on both sides of the matrix.
        Key terms of this lesson
        Retention periodHow long a record is kept before destruction or anonymization; counted from a trigger event.
        Legal minimum / legal maximumKeep at least (tax, PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) logs, breach registers) / keep no longer than necessary (privacy laws).
        Retention scheduleThe table that applies the retention policy record type by record type (7 columns).
        TriggerThe event that starts the retention clock (end of tax year, account closure, last activity, recording date).
        Legal holdSuspension of destruction when a dispute, complaint or investigation is reasonably anticipated.
        AnonymizationIrreversible transformation so that the person can no longer be identified; under Law 25 it follows the 2024 regulation and is an alternative to destruction.

        Code illustration — L4_retention_schedule.py (Python 3)
        

        Task of the code: Read L4_retention_schedule.csv (five record types with legal minimum in months, a maximum reference in months, the period applied today and a sample trigger date), compute the disposal date of each record type, compare the applied period with the minimum and the maximum, and print the schedule with a flag per row.
        Relation to the lecture: Illustrates sections 4.1–4.3: the minimum / maximum comparison and the schedule columns. The two flags are the two retention non-conformities an auditor reports.
        Run it: python3 L4_retention_schedule.py · data file: L4_retention_schedule.csv
        

        
 
        L4_retention_schedule.py
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
        
 
        
  
        1# csv reads the schedule file; date and timedelta compute disposal dates from the trigger date.2import csv3# date for the trigger, timedelta is not enough for months, so we add months by arithmetic on year and month fields.4from datetime import date5# A helper that adds n months to a date: months are not a fixed number of days, so we move the year and month fields and keep the day (capped at 28 for safety).6def add_months(d, n):7#     Total months since year 0, plus n, then split back into year and month.8    y, m = divmod(d.year * 12 + (d.month - 1) + n, 12)9#     Rebuild the date; min(d.day, 28) avoids an invalid day such as February 30.10    return date(y, m + 1, min(d.day, 28))11# Open the schedule file; one row per record type.12with open("L4_retention_schedule.csv", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:13#     Read every row as a dictionary keyed by the column names.14    rows = list(csv.DictReader(f))15# Print the header of the schedule we are about to produce.16print(f"{'Record type':<24} {'Min':>4} {'Max':>4} {'Now':>4}  {'Disposal':<10} Flag")17# Counters for the two non-conformity types, reported at the end.18too_early = too_long = 019# Loop over the five record types.20for r in rows:21#     Convert the three periods (months) from text to integers; 0 for the maximum means 'no legal maximum applies' (no personal information).22    mn, mx, now = int(r["min_months"]), int(r["max_months"]), int(r["applied_months"])23#     Parse the sample trigger date written as YYYY-MM-DD.24    trig = date.fromisoformat(r["trigger_date"])25#     The disposal date is the trigger date plus the period actually applied today.26    disposal = add_months(trig, now) if now > 0 else None27#     Default flag: the practice is acceptable.28    flag = "OK"29#     Destroyed too early: the applied period is shorter than the legal minimum (for example logs rotated after 1 month when 12 are required).30    if now < mn:31#         Record the violated minimum rule in the flag and count it.32        flag = f"TOO EARLY (< {mn} months, {r['min_basis']})"; too_early += 133#     Kept too long: a maximum applies (mx > 0) and the applied period exceeds it — 'forever' is written as 9999 in the file.34    elif mx and now > mx:35#         Record the violated maximum rule and count it.36        flag = f"TOO LONG (> {mx} months, {r['max_basis']})"; too_long += 137#     Print the row: 9999 is displayed as 'inf' (kept indefinitely) and a missing disposal date as a dash.38    print(f"{r['record_type']:<24} {mn:>4} {('inf' if mx==9999 else mx or '-'):>4} {('inf' if now==9999 else now):>4}  {str(disposal) if disposal and now != 9999 else '-':<10} {flag}")39# Summary line: how many rows of each non-conformity type; both go to Project Section 7.40print(f"\nNon-conformities: {too_early} destroyed too early, {too_long} kept too long — {len(rows) - too_early - too_long} row(s) conform")

          Step-by-step explanation
          1. Each line of the CSV is one record type with four numbers: the legal minimum in months, the maximum reference in months (0 when no maximum applies, 9999 for ‘indefinitely’), the period the company applies today, and a sample trigger date.
          2. add_months moves a date forward by a number of months; months have different lengths, so the function works on the year and month fields rather than on days.
          3. For each row the script computes the disposal date (trigger + applied period), then compares the applied period with the minimum (too early) and with the maximum (too long). The flag names the rule violated, so the finding is already written.
          4. The counters give the summary an auditor puts in the executive summary: how many record types are destroyed too early, how many are kept too long.
          5. The visualization is a timeline per record type: a green zone between the minimum and the maximum, and a marker for the period applied today — left of the zone means too early, right of it means too long.

          Flash cards — click a card to reveal the answer
          Legal minimum vs legal maximum
          Minimum = keep at least (CRA (Canada Revenue Agency) / Revenu Québec 6 years, PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) logs 12 months, breach register 24 months, incident register 5 years). Maximum = keep no longer than necessary (PIPEDA (Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act) 4.5, Law 25 s. 23, GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) 5(1)(e)).
          Which wins when they conflict?
          The legal minimum, for as long as it lasts (the privacy laws except retention periods fixed by law); afterwards the maximum applies and the record must be destroyed or anonymized.
          PCI DSS 3.2.1 and 10.5.1
          3.2.1 = account-data retention and disposal policy, with a check at least every three months that expired data is gone. 10.5.1 = audit logs kept at least 12 months, the most recent 3 months immediately available.
          The seven columns of a retention schedule
          Record type (PI (personal information)? card data?) · legal basis (min and max) · retention period · trigger · disposal method · owner · exceptions (legal hold).
          The two retention non-conformities
          Destroyed too early (below a legal minimum) and kept too long (past the purpose without a legal basis).

          5
          Mapping organizational policies to legal and regulatory requirements — the traceability matrix and crosswalks
          ≈ 8 min · Lesson 5 of 6
          

          Learning objectives — after this lesson you can:
          • Build one row of a traceability matrix: requirement → policy clause → control → evidence → test.
          • Name the three gap types a matrix reveals (policy gap, implementation gap, evidence gap).
          • Use a crosswalk (CIS ↔ CSF ↔ ISO ↔ PCI DSS) so that one piece of evidence satisfies several frameworks.
          • Describe what Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager automates (demo only).
          5.1 Why mapping is the heart of a conformity assessment
          

          A law states a requirement (“keep personal information only as long as necessary”). A company answers with a policy clause (“Privacy Policy §6: accounts inactive for 24 months are deleted”). The clause is implemented by a control (a monthly deletion job in the web store). The control leaves evidence (the job’s log, a screenshot of the configuration, a count of deleted accounts). The auditor applies a test to the evidence (re-performance: run the query; observation: watch the job run). A traceability matrix is the table that keeps these five elements on one line per requirement, so that every requirement can be traced forward to its proof and every piece of evidence traced back to the requirement it serves.
          

          Without the matrix, an assessment is a pile of screenshots. With it, the Project’s Section 6 writes itself: each finding is one line of the matrix with a result.
          5.2 The columns and the three gap types
          

          ColumnContentExample (Érable Cycles)
          

          Req ID (identifier)Your own identifierR-04
          

          SourceLaw / standard and articlePCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) v4.0.1 — 8.3.6
          

          RequirementIn plain wordsPasswords of at least 12 characters with letters and numbers
          

          Policy & clauseThe company document that states itAccess Control Policy §4.2 — draft
          

          ControlThe mechanism that enforces itActive Directory password policy; Microsoft 365 password settings
          

          Evidence to collectWhat proves the control worksnet accounts output; Microsoft 365 authentication-methods screenshot
          

          Test (Lab 3)How you will checkRe-performance on the Windows VM (virtual machine); document review of the policy status
          

          Framework referencesCrosswalkCIS (Center for Internet Security) 5.2 · CSF (Cybersecurity Framework) PR.AA-01 · ISO (International Organization for Standardization) A.5.17
          

          

          Reading the matrix line by line exposes three kinds of gap:
          

            

          • Policy gap — a requirement with no approved policy clause (R-04 above: the Access Control Policy is a draft, so the requirement is unsupported even if the technical setting happens to be right).
            • 

          • Implementation gap — a policy clause with no control that enforces it (the Privacy Policy promises deletion after 24 months; no job exists).
            • 

          • Evidence gap — a control that exists but leaves no proof (backups run, but no restore test record; training happens, but no attendance log). For an auditor, a control without evidence is treated as not operating.
            • 

          5.3 Crosswalks — test once, satisfy many
          

          Because the frameworks overlap, the same control and the same evidence usually satisfy several of them. A crosswalk (also called a mapping) is a table that lists, for one item of a framework, the matching items of the others. Three free crosswalks cover everything this course needs: the CIS Controls v8.1 mappings (to CSF 2.0, ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission) 27001:2022, PCI DSS v4.0, SP (Special Publication) 800-53 Rev. 5) and the CIS Controls Navigator; the NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) OLIR (Online Informative References) / CPRT (Cybersecurity and Privacy Reference Tool) Informative References of the CSF 2.0; and the ISO/IEC 27002:2022 attributes, whose “cybersecurity concepts” column is literally the CSF Functions.
          

          Requirement (source)CIS v8.1 SafeguardCSF 2.0ISO/IEC 27001:2022One piece of evidence
          

          Password length ≥ 12 (PCI DSS 8.3.6)5.2 Use unique passwordsPR.AA-01A.5.17 Authentication informationnet accounts + policy screenshot
          

          Logs kept 12 months (PCI DSS 10.5.1)8.3 Ensure adequate audit log storagePR.PS-04A.8.15 Logginglogrotate / event-log settings
          

          Retention limited to purpose (PIPEDA (Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act) 4.5, Law 25 s. 23, GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) 5(1)(e))3.4 Enforce data retentionGV.PO-01 / PR.DSA.5.33 Protection of records · A.8.10 Information deletionRetention schedule + deletion-job log
          

          Breach notification (PIPEDA 10.1, Law 25 s. 3.5, GDPR 33)17.1–17.3 Incident responseRS.CO-02A.5.24–A.5.26 Incident managementIncident procedure + register
          

          Least privilege (PCI DSS 7.2, Law 25 s. 10)6.1 / 6.2 Access granting and revokingPR.AA-05A.5.15 · A.5.18 Access rightsAccess-review extract; local admin lists
          

          Secure configuration (PCI DSS 2.2)4.1 Secure configuration processPR.PS-01A.8.9 Configuration managementCIS-CAT (CIS Configuration Assessment Tool) Lite report; Lynis report
          

          

          The rule that follows: collect the evidence once, name the file once (L3-E07_net-accounts.png) and reference it in every framework column. Your evidence index in the CPM (Course Procedure Manual) is the list of those unique names.
          5.4 Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager — what a tool automates (instructor demo)
          

          Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager, included in Microsoft 365 Business Premium (the Érable Cycles tenant), does the matrix work at the scale of hundreds of requirements. It offers assessment templates for regulations and standards (ISO/IEC 27001, NIST CSF, PCI DSS, GDPR, PIPEDA and Québec’s private-sector privacy law, among many others), lists improvement actions for each, computes a compliance score and — the point of this lesson — shares one action and its evidence across all the assessments it satisfies. Intune compliance policies and MECM (Microsoft Endpoint Configuration Manager) configuration baselines do the same at device level: one baseline, reported against several controls. You will see both as screenshots; nobody installs them.
          Key terms of this lesson
          Traceability matrixA table with one line per requirement: source → requirement → policy clause → control → evidence → test → framework references.
          Policy gap / implementation gap / evidence gapNo approved clause for a requirement / no control for a clause / no proof for a control.
          Crosswalk (mapping)A table linking one framework’s items to the equivalent items of other frameworks (CIS (Center for Internet Security) ↔ CSF (Cybersecurity Framework) ↔ ISO (International Organization for Standardization) ↔ PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard)).
          Test once, satisfy manyCollect one piece of evidence, name it once, reference it in every framework column it satisfies.
          Compliance ManagerMicrosoft Purview feature: assessment templates, improvement actions, compliance score, shared evidence across assessments (demo only).

            Step-by-step explanation
            1. The page stores the eight requirements as JavaScript objects: source article, requirement in plain words, the policy clause (and whether that policy is approved), the control, the evidence file name and the crosswalk references.
            2. The status() function is the whole lesson in four tests, applied in order: no approved clause → policy gap; clause without a control → implementation gap; control without evidence → evidence gap; otherwise supported. Order matters: a draft policy is a policy gap even if the technical setting is right (R-04).
            3. The loop adds one table row per requirement, colours it by status and increments a counter.
            4. The last line prints the coverage: 4 supported out of 8, 2 policy gaps (R-04, R-05), 1 implementation gap (R-02), 1 evidence gap (R-08). Those four gaps are the draft non-conformities of Project Section 7.
            5. The visualization is the matrix itself filling in row by row with its colours, which is exactly what you do in the Lab 1 workbook tonight.

            Requirement → policy clause → control → evidence → test. A break at the first link is a policy gap, at the second an implementation gap, at the third an evidence gap.

            Flash cards — click a card to reveal the answer
            The five elements of one matrix line
            Requirement (what is demanded) → policy clause (what the company says) → control (the mechanism) → evidence (the proof) → test (how the auditor checks).
            The three gap types
            Policy gap: requirement with no approved clause. Implementation gap: clause with no control. Evidence gap: control with no proof — treated as not operating.
            What is a crosswalk?
            A table that links one framework’s items to the equivalent items of others (CIS (Center for Internet Security) Controls v8.1 mappings, NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) OLIR (Online Informative References) / CPRT (Cybersecurity and Privacy Reference Tool), ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission) 27002 attributes). Purpose: test once, satisfy many.
            Why is a draft policy a policy gap?
            A draft is not approved, so the requirement has no authorized support even if the technical setting is correct (R-04: password length).
            What does Compliance Manager automate?
            Assessment templates per regulation, improvement actions, a compliance score, and one action / evidence shared across all the assessments it satisfies (demo only).

            6
            Documentation requirements for regulatory compliance — documents, records, evidence
            ≈ 8 min · Lesson 6 of 6
            

            Learning objectives — after this lesson you can:
            • Distinguish a document (policy, procedure) from a record (evidence of an activity).
            • List the document-control attributes an auditor checks (identification, version, date, approval, review, communication).
            • Name the records the Day 2 laws and PCI DSS require Érable Cycles to keep.
            • Apply the five-question policy check and the rules of good audit evidence; connect them to the Course Procedure Manual.
            6.1 Documents and records — two kinds of documented information
            

            ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission) 27001 clause 7.5 uses one term, documented information, for two different things. Documents state intent and rules: policies (what and why), procedures (who does what, step by step), standards and guidelines. They are maintained: kept current through reviews. Records are evidence that an activity happened: an access-review sheet, a training attendance list, an incident register entry, a backup log, a signed consent. They are retained: kept unchanged for a retention period (Lesson 4). An auditor needs both: the document tells what should happen, the record proves that it did.
            

            The sentence to remember is “if it isn’t documented, it didn’t happen”. It is not cynicism; it is the definition of audit evidence. ISO (International Organization for Standardization) 19011 asks evidence to be sufficient (enough of it), reliable (from a trustworthy source — a system output over a verbal statement) and relevant (about the requirement being tested).
            6.2 Document control — what an auditor checks on every policy
            

            Clause 7.5.2 and 7.5.3 of ISO/IEC 27001 list the attributes of a controlled document. In practice the auditor checks six things on the first page of every policy:
            

              

            1. Identification — title, unique reference, owner.
              2. 

            2. Version — number and change history.
              3. 

            3. Date — of issue and of the next planned review (PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) 12.1.2: security policies are reviewed at least once every 12 months and updated when the environment changes).
              4. 

            4. Approval — by whom, when; a draft has no authority (the Access Control Policy of the case file).
              5. 

            5. Communication — how staff learned of it: publication location, training, acknowledgement; Law 25 section 3.2 goes further for privacy governance policies — they must be published on the website in simple and clear terms, with the title and contact of the person in charge (section 3.1).
              6. 

            6. Application — the records that prove it is followed (tickets, reviews, logs).
              7. 

            

            These six points are the five-question policy check of Lab 3 (exists / approved / dated and versioned / communicated / applied with evidence) — the sixth, identification, is the precondition for the other five.
            6.3 Records the law requires Érable Cycles to keep
            

            TextRecord (minimum content)Retention
            

            PIPEDA (Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act)Breach records (every breach, with the assessment of real risk of significant harm) · consents · privacy policies and practices available on request (Principle 4.8 Openness)Breach records 24 months
            

            Law 25Published governance policies · title and contact of the person in charge · PIA (privacy impact assessment) reports · confidentiality-incident register · privacy-by-default settingsRegister entries 5 years
            

            GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation)ROPA (record of processing activities) (Article 30) · breach documentation (Article 33(5)) · DPIA (data protection impact assessment) where required (Article 35) · proof of consent (Article 7)While processing continues; breach documentation for supervisory review
            

            PCI DSS v4.0.1Policies reviewed annually (12.1.2) · roles and responsibilities (12.1.3) · training records (12.6) · quarterly account-data retention checks (3.2.1) · log reviews (10.4) · the SAQ (Self-Assessment Questionnaire) and attestation of compliancePer the merchant agreement; logs 12 months
            

            CASL (Canada’s Anti-Spam Legislation)Proof of consent (section 13) · unsubscribe requests and the date they took effectLife of the consent + 3 years (limitation)
            

            6.4 Evidence rules for this course — and the Course Procedure Manual
            

              

            • Every evidence file has a unique name: L3-E07_net-accounts.png (lab, evidence number, content). It appears once in the evidence index and is referenced from the matrix and the findings table.
              • 

            • Screenshots show the hostname and the date; real personal information is masked (Legal Notice section 18.2).
              • 

            • “Not tested — reason: …” is an acceptable record; an invented screenshot fails the item and breaks the academic-integrity rules.
              • 

            • Your Course Procedure Manual is documented information in the ISO sense — the implementation of control A.5.37 Documented operating procedures for the audit itself. Each procedure follows the 7-line skeleton (purpose · prerequisites · numbered steps with exact commands · expected output · interpretation · evidence to keep · common problems). Chapter 1, written this week, documents how you built the register, the matrix and the retention schedule.
              • 

            Key terms of this lesson
            Documented informationISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission) 27001 7.5 term covering documents (policies, procedures — maintained) and records (evidence — retained).
            Document controlIdentification, version, date, approval, review cycle, communication and protection of a document (7.5.2, 7.5.3).
            RecordEvidence that an activity happened (access review, training list, incident entry, backup log, consent); kept unchanged for its retention period.
            Sufficient, reliable, relevantISO (International Organization for Standardization) 19011 qualities of audit evidence: enough of it, from a trustworthy source, about the requirement tested.
            Five-question policy checkExists? approved? dated and versioned? communicated? applied with evidence? — used in Lab 3 on the case-file policies.
            Evidence indexThe list of uniquely named evidence files (L3-E07_…) referenced by the matrix, the findings and the CPM (Course Procedure Manual).
