            Real-life example — The document register of Érable Cycles passed through the six checks
            

            Task of this example: List the six policies and procedures of the case file, the backup procedure written by the MSP and two legally required records in a nine-line document register (version, status, approver, approval date, review cycle, last review, communicated, acknowledgement rate), run the six document-control checks on each line, and compute a documentation-readiness figure.
            Relation to the lecture: Applies sections 6.1 and 6.2: the document-control attributes and the five-question policy check. The flagged lines are the administrative findings of Lab 3.
            

            Part of future labs:Lab 3 — administrative controls — the 5-question checklist applied to the case-file policies starts from this registerLab 1 — Part B.2 — the ‘policy & clause’ column must point to an approved document; a draft is a policy gapCPM — front matter — the conventions page (naming, masking, version) is the document control of your own manual
            

            The audit team asks the IT (information technology) administrator for the first page of every policy and for the two registers the law requires. Nine lines go into the register. Three problems appear at once: the Access Control Policy is a draft without an approver; the Patch Management Procedure was last reviewed in 2024 and its 12-month review is overdue; the Acceptable Use Policy was communicated, but only 61 % of the 45 employees acknowledged it. The incident register exists but is empty — which is a finding only if an incident happened, so it is marked for interview. The readiness figure the team computes (documents with zero issues over total) goes into the executive summary next to the technical scores.
            Deliverables of the example:
            • A 9-line document register with the six checks applied
            • A list of issues per document (draft, no approval date, review overdue, not communicated, low acknowledgement)
            • A documentation-readiness percentage for the executive summary
            


            Code illustration — L6_Test-DocumentControl.ps1 (PowerShell 7)
            

            Task of the code: Read L6_document_register.csv (nine documents and records), check each line for the document-control issues (draft, missing approval date, review overdue as of today, not communicated, acknowledgement below 90 %), print the issues and compute the documentation-readiness percentage.
            Relation to the lecture: Illustrates section 6.2: the six checks an auditor runs on every policy, as a repeatable script. The output is the starting point of the administrative review of Lab 3.
            Run it: pwsh -File L6_Test-DocumentControl.ps1  (or run in Windows PowerShell 5.1) · data file: L6_document_register.csv
            

            
 
            L6_Test-DocumentControl.ps1
  
  
  
  
  
  
  
            
 
            
  
            1# Fix the audit date so that everyone obtains the same result in class; in real use: Get-Date.2$today = Get-Date "2026-11-03"3# Read the register: one object per document with the columns Document, Type, Version, Status, ApprovedBy, ApprovedOn, ReviewMonths, LastReview, Communicated, AckPct.4$docs = Import-Csv -Path "L6_document_register.csv"5# Counter of documents with no issue at all, used for the readiness figure.6$clean = 07# Loop over every line of the register.8foreach ($d in $docs) {9#     Start with an empty list of issues for this document.10    $issues = @()11#     Check 1 — approval: a Draft has no authority (Access Control Policy).12    if ($d.Status -eq "Draft") { $issues += "draft, not approved" }13#     Check 2 — approval date: an approved document must carry the date of approval.14    if ($d.Status -eq "Approved" -and [string]::IsNullOrWhiteSpace($d.ApprovedOn)) { $issues += "no approval date" }15#     Check 3 — review cycle: compute the due date = last review + review cycle in months; overdue if before today (PCI DSS 12.1.2 → 12 months for security policies).16    if ($d.LastReview) { $due = ([datetime]$d.LastReview).AddMonths([int]$d.ReviewMonths); if ($due -lt $today) { $issues += ("review overdue since {0:yyyy-MM-dd}" -f $due) } }17#     Check 4 — communication: a policy nobody was told about cannot be applied (records are exempt from this check).18    if ($d.Type -ne "Record" -and $d.Communicated -ne "Y") { $issues += "not communicated" }19#     Check 5 — acknowledgement: below 90 % of staff is treated as incomplete communication (the threshold is the team's, written in the plan).20    if ($d.Type -ne "Record" -and [int]$d.AckPct -lt 90) { $issues += ("acknowledged by {0}% only" -f $d.AckPct) }21#     If the list is empty the document passes all checks: count it as clean and print OK.22    if ($issues.Count -eq 0) { $clean++; Write-Output ("OK    {0} v{1}" -f $d.Document, $d.Version) }23#     Otherwise print the document name followed by its issues, separated by semicolons.24    else { Write-Output ("ISSUE {0} v{1}: {2}" -f $d.Document, $d.Version, ($issues -join "; ")) }25# End of the loop.26}27# Readiness = clean documents over total, as a whole percentage.28$readiness = [math]::Round(($clean / $docs.Count) * 100)29# Print the figure for the executive summary.30Write-Output ("Documentation readiness: {0}/{1} documents without issue = {2}%" -f $clean, $docs.Count, $readiness)
            
  
            
   
            Execution steps — click a step to jump to it; pause to discuss
              
   
              Variables at this step: 
              
   
              
  
              
 
              
 
              

              

              Step-by-step explanation
              1. The register CSV has one line per document or record with the attributes an auditor reads on a first page: version, status, approver and date, review cycle, last review, communication and acknowledgement rate.
              2. Five checks run on each line, in the order of the five-question policy check: approval (draft?), approval date, review overdue (last review + cycle compared with today), communication, acknowledgement. Records skip the two communication checks because they are evidence, not rules.
              3. A document with an empty issue list is ‘clean’; the readiness figure is the share of clean documents. It is one number the CEO can follow, like the IG1 coverage of Lesson 3.
              4. The expected output flags the Access Control Policy (draft), the Patch Management Procedure (review overdue) and the Acceptable Use Policy (61 % acknowledgement); the incident register passes the checks and is marked for interview in the lab.
              5. The visualization is the register as a table whose status cells turn green or red as the checks run, with the readiness gauge updating at the end.
              


              Figure 6 — The life of a controlled document and the records it produces
              Draft → review → approval → publication and communication → application (records) → periodic review (12 months) → revision or retirement. The auditor checks the attributes on the first page and the records at the end of the chain.
